stages.title: Materials and objects around us
stages.hook: Look at your chair, your cup and your shoe. Are they made of the same stuff? What is each one made of?
explain: An object is a thing you can hold or see, like a spoon. A material is the stuff the object is made of. A spoon can be made of metal, wood or plastic.
People pick a material because of how it behaves. A cup must hold water, so we do not make it from paper that melts into mush. A window must let light in, so we use glass.
Some materials come from nature, like wood, wool and stone. Some are made by people, like plastic and glass. Looking closely at materials is the first step of chemistry.

example.q: A rain coat keeps you dry. Which material is best: cloth that soaks up water, or plastic that water slides off?
steps: Think about the job: the coat must keep water out.
Cloth that soaks up water would get wet.
Plastic lets water slide off.

analogies.home: In a kitchen, spoons, plates and pans are objects. Metal, clay and wood are the materials they are made of.
analogies.farm: A bucket can be metal or plastic. A fence can be wood or wire. The farmer chooses what suits the job.
analogies.city: Roads are made of stone and tar, windows of glass and buses of metal.
analogies.nature: A bird nest is an object. Its materials are twigs, grass and mud.

stages.mnemonic: Object is the thing. Material is the stuff. A cup is the thing, clay is the stuff.
terms: A thing you can see or hold.
What an object is made of.
Comes from plants, animals or the ground.

misc.wrong: A material and an object are the same thing.
misc.right: An object is the thing, and a material is what it is made of. One material, like wood, can make many objects.

stages.limits: Many objects use more than one material, like a pencil with wood, graphite and rubber.

stages.title: Solids, liquids and gases
stages.hook: Ice, water and steam are all the same stuff. Why do they look and feel so different?
explain: There are three main states of matter. A solid keeps its shape, like a stone. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its cup, like water. A gas spreads out to fill all the space, like air in a balloon.
Everything is made of tiny bits too small to see. In a solid the bits stay close and stay in place. In a liquid they slide past each other. In a gas they zoom around far apart.
You can pour a liquid, but you cannot pour a stone. You cannot see most gases, but you can feel the wind.

example.q: Is juice in a glass a solid, a liquid or a gas?
steps: Juice flows when you tip the glass.
It takes the shape of the glass.
Things that flow and fill the bottom of a cup are liquids.

analogies.home: A cup of tea is a liquid, a spoon is a solid and steam over the cup is a gas.
analogies.sport: A football is a solid. The air inside it is a gas.
analogies.nature: A lake is liquid, ice on a mountain is solid and mist is water in the air.
analogies.sea: The sea is liquid, an iceberg is solid and sea air holds water as a gas.

stages.mnemonic: Solid stays. Liquid flows. Gas goes everywhere.
terms: Flows and takes the shape of its container.
Spreads out to fill any space.
Whether something is solid, liquid or gas.

misc.wrong: A powder like sand is a liquid because it pours.
misc.right: Each grain of sand is a tiny solid. A pile of grains pours but the grains keep their shape.

stages.limits: There are other states too, like plasma, but we study three first.

stages.title: Colours, textures and material properties
stages.hook: Close your eyes and touch a stone, a sponge and a sheet of paper. How can you tell them apart?
explain: A property is something we can say about a material. Colour, shininess and texture are properties. Texture means how it feels, like rough, smooth or soft.
Other properties are hard or soft, bendy or stiff, and whether water goes through. Some materials float and some sink. We use our senses to find them out.
Properties help us pick materials. A towel is soft and soaks up water. A saucepan is hard and does not melt on the stove.

example.q: You need something to wipe up spilt water. A sponge or a plastic ruler?
steps: Wiping up needs a material that soaks up water.
A sponge is soft and soaks up water.
A plastic ruler is hard and does not soak up water.

analogies.home: A pillow is soft, a table is hard and a mirror is shiny.
analogies.farm: Wool is soft and warm. A wire fence is strong and rough.
analogies.sport: A tennis ball is bouncy. A cricket bat is hard and stiff.
analogies.music: A drum skin is stretchy. A bell is hard and shiny, and it rings.

stages.mnemonic: Look, touch, test. Colour, feel, strong, best.
terms: Something we can say about a material.

misc.right: Some big heavy things float, like a wooden log. What matters is the material, not only how big the object is.

stages.limits: Our senses are useful but cannot tell everything, so scientists also use tools to measure.

stages.title: Mixing and separating materials
stages.hook: If you mix sand and little stones in a bucket, how could you get them apart again?
explain: A mixture is two or more things put together. In a mixture each part keeps being itself. Salad, trail mix and sand with stones are mixtures.
Many mixtures can be separated. A sieve has holes: small bits fall through and big bits stay. A magnet pulls out iron. A filter paper lets water through but not sand.
We pick a way that matches a difference. The difference might be size, or that one part is magnetic.

example.q: Rice and small stones are mixed. How can you separate them?
steps: Look for a difference: the stones are bigger than rice grains.
Pick a sieve with holes that let rice pass but not stones.
Shake it. Rice falls through and stones stay.

analogies.sea: A net lets water through but keeps fish.

misc.right: A mixture keeps its parts, so it can often be separated again.

stages.title: Safe observation of everyday changes
stages.hook: A banana goes brown and an ice cube goes wet. Are these the same kind of change?
explain: Things around us change. Some changes can be undone. Ice melts, and water can freeze again. Some changes cannot be undone. Toast does not turn back into bread.
When we watch changes we use our eyes, and we stay safe. We never taste or smell unknown things. We never touch hot things. We ask a grown-up.
Signs of a new material forming can be a new colour, a new smell, bubbles or heat. Look and write down what you see.

example.q: Wax from a candle goes soft in the sun and hard again in the shade. Can this change be undone?
steps: Wax goes soft when warm.
It goes hard when cool.
It goes back and forth, so it is a change that can be undone.

stages.title: Heating and cooling
stages.hook: Why does chocolate melt in the sun but a stone does not?
explain: Heat is energy that moves from hot things to cooler things. When a material gets hot, its tiny bits move faster. When it gets cold, they move slower.
Heating can make a solid melt into a liquid. Heating a liquid can make it turn to a gas. Cooling does the opposite. Steam cools into water and water freezes into ice.
Different materials need different amounts of heat. Chocolate melts at a low temperature. A stone needs very much more. A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius.

example.q: Water in a puddle goes down on a sunny day. Where does it go?
steps: Sun heats the puddle.
Warm water turns into a gas called water vapour.
The vapour goes into the air.
example.a: It becomes water vapour in the air

stages.title: Dissolving substances in water
stages.hook: Stir a spoon of sugar in warm water and it vanishes. Where did it go?
explain: When sugar or salt mixes into water and seems to disappear, we say it dissolves. The tiny bits spread out among the water and are too small to see. Water with something dissolved in it is a solution.
The sugar is not gone. We never taste to find out. We can show it is there because the water boils away and leaves it behind.
Not everything dissolves. Sand does not dissolve in water. It sinks to the bottom. Warm water usually dissolves things faster, and stirring helps too.

example.q: Salt is stirred in water and the water looks clear. Is the salt still there?
steps: The salt breaks up into bits too small to see.
They spread through the water.
The water looks clear but the salt is still there.

stages.title: Everyday metals, plastics and ceramics
stages.hook: A metal spoon, a plastic spoon and a clay bowl all sit on a table. Why are they so different?
explain: Metals are usually hard, shiny and strong. They feel cold because they carry heat away from your hand fast. Many metals also let electricity pass through them, so wires are made of metal.

Plastics are made by people, often from oil. They are light, can be bent or moulded into any shape and many do not let water through. Ceramics are made from clay baked in a hot oven called a kiln. They are hard but break if dropped.
Each group suits different jobs. A metal wire carries electricity, a plastic bottle holds a drink and a ceramic mug keeps tea hot.

example.q: A cooking pot must be strong and handle heat. Which group suits it: metal, plastic or paper?
steps: The pot gets very hot.
Plastic and paper would melt or burn.
Metal is strong and carries heat.

terms: A hard shiny material that carries heat and electricity.

A hard material made by baking clay.

misc.right: There are many kinds of plastic with different properties, such as stiff or bendy.

stages.limits: Some objects mix groups, and some ceramics are very tough, like those on spacecraft.

questions.q: Why are a kettle's handle and body made from different materials?
o: The body must be hot, the handle must not be
questions.why: Each part suits its job.

questions.q: Which is best for a bicycle frame that must be strong?
questions.why: Metals are strong.

panel.q: Why is wire plastic-coated on the outside?
o: Plastic stops electricity reaching your hand
Plastic is pretty to look at
Metal is never safe to carry
panel.why: Plastic does not let electricity pass.

panel.q: Which is better for a fireproof tile?
Can we recycle metal, plastic and glass?
o: Yes, many can be collected and reused
No, they can never be reused

teach.model: Metals are hard, shiny and carry heat and electricity. Plastics are light and can be moulded. Ceramics are baked clay, hard but they can break.

stages.title: Laboratory safety
stages.hook: Why do scientists wear goggles and tie back their hair, even for a small test?
explain: A lab is a place for careful tests. The first rule is to listen to the grown-up in charge. The second is to wear safety goggles and keep long hair tied back.
Never taste, never smell strong things and never mix things unless you are told. Keep your place tidy and wash your hands after. Tell a grown-up at once if something spills or breaks.
We read the label on a container. Signs and symbols warn us about danger. Many safe tests use things like water, sugar and salt.

example.q: A glass cup falls and breaks on the floor. What should you do?
steps: Stay still and do not touch the pieces.
Tell the grown-up straight away.
Let them clear it up safely.
example.a: Tell a grown-up and do not touch the pieces

analogies.home: In a kitchen we wear oven gloves and ask for help with hot pots. A lab has rules like that.
analogies.sport: Players wear helmets and pads to stay safe, like goggles in a lab.
analogies.city: Traffic lights and signs keep roads safe, as warning signs do in labs.
analogies.farm: A farmer wears boots and gloves and keeps tools in the right place.

stages.mnemonic: Goggles on, hair tied back, listen well, stay on track.
terms: Words on a container that say what is inside.
When liquid gets out of its container.

misc.wrong: Safety rules are only for dangerous experiments.
misc.right: We follow safety rules every time, even for easy tests.

stages.limits: This is a first idea. Real labs have many more rules.

trip.prompt: Find a safety sign or tool in the pictures and say what it protects.

questions.q: What should you do with long hair in a lab?

Do it quickly so no one sees

teach.topic: How to stay safe in a lab
teach.model: Listen to the grown-up. Wear goggles and tie back hair. Never taste or smell unknown things. Tell a grown-up if something spills or breaks, and wash your hands at the end.
